Haste
hast
n. and v. (speed, urgency; hurried and often unadvised movement; rendering Hebrew chippazon and mahar, Greek spoude)
From Old French haste, of Germanic origin, akin to the Saxon haest, violence or vehemence. The old sense carried more heat than mere speed — haste was hurry with agitation in it, which is why the KJV can set it against faith.

Biblical Definition

Scripture divides haste exactly, and the division is worth learning. There is a commanded haste, and there is a condemned one. At the first passover Israel ate “with your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and ye shall eat it in haste” (Exodus 12:11) — redemption is an errand to be obeyed at once, and the posture of the meal preached the urgency of the deliverance. But haste born of unbelief is another thing. David confesses, “I said in my haste, I am cut off from before thine eyes” (Psalm 31:22), and the verse is an honest record of a conclusion reached too fast under pressure; the next clause overturns it, nevertheless thou heardest. Proverbs makes it a moral matter: “he that hasteth with his feet sinneth” (Proverbs 19:2), the feet outrunning the knowledge the previous clause says the soul lacks. And Isaiah puts the definitive word beside the cornerstone: “he that believeth shall not make haste” (Isaiah 28:16). That is not a commendation of sloth. It means that the man whose foundation is a tried stone laid by God has no need of panic; he can wait, because his security does not depend on his own speed. Faith produces a certain unhurriedness that unbelief can never counterfeit.

Webster 1828 Definition

Speed, urgency, hurry. Scripture commands it at the passover and condemns it in the anxious heart, setting Isaiah's rule over both: he that believeth shall not make haste.

expand to see more

HASTE, n. [Fr. hate; Sax. haest, violence.] Celerity of motion; speed; swiftness; dispatch; expedition.

2. Sudden excitement of passion; vehemence; precipitance.

3. The state of being urged or pressed by business; as, to be in haste.

4. HASTE, v.t. To press; to drive or urge forward; to push on.

5. HASTE, v.i. To move with celerity; to be rapid in motion.

Key Scripture

Exodus 12:11 — "And thus shall ye eat it; with your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and ye shall eat it in haste: it is the LORD'S passover."

Psalm 31:22 — "For I said in my haste, I am cut off from before thine eyes: nevertheless thou heardest the voice of my supplications when I cried unto thee."

Proverbs 19:2 — "Also, that the soul be without knowledge, it is not good; and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth."

Isaiah 28:16 — "Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste."

Modern Corruption

Speed is treated as a virtue in itself and slowness as failure, so that hurry is never examined for what usually drives it — unbelief that God will act unless we act first.

expand to see more

An age that measures everything by how quickly it arrives has no way to hear Isaiah 28:16. To be told that believing men do not make haste sounds like a rebuke of diligence, and it is not; Scripture commands promptness in obedience often enough, and the passover was eaten standing. What Isaiah rebukes is the hurry that comes from having no foundation. The context is a people making desperate arrangements — a covenant with death, a refuge of lies — because they will not trust the stone God is laying in Zion. Panic is what unbelief looks like when it is busy. The remedy is not a slower schedule but a surer foundation.

The principle to recover is that haste is a symptom to be read rather than a pace to be praised or blamed on its own. David's I said in my haste (Psalm 31:22) is the most useful phrase in the Psalter for this, because it lets a believer put a date on a false conclusion without disowning himself. Under pressure he concluded he was cut off; the conclusion was wrong; God heard him anyway. Every Christian has said something in his haste. Wisdom is not pretending otherwise, but learning to hold such verdicts loosely until the pulse has slowed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chippazon is hurried flight, the word of the passover; mahar is to hasten or be rash. Greek spoude is diligence or speed, and speudo, to hasten.

expand to see more

Hebrew chippazon (H2649) — hurried flight, trepidation; used of eating the passover in haste.

Hebrew mahar (H4116) — to hasten, to be rash or precipitate; often carrying blame.

Hebrew chush (H2363) — to hurry, to make speed; used both of eager obedience and of panic.

Greek spoude (G4710) — haste, earnestness, diligence; Mary went into the hill country with haste.

Greek speudo (G4692) — to hasten, to urge on; the shepherds came with haste to Bethlehem.

Usage

"Of commanded urgency in redemption: ye shall eat it in haste: it is the LORD'S passover (Exodus 12:11)."

"Of a false conclusion reached under pressure: I said in my haste, I am cut off from before thine eyes (Psalm 31:22)."

"Of the unhurriedness faith produces: he that believeth shall not make haste (Isaiah 28:16)."
